description: Two-person team. Guillermo: aerospace background; builds AI assistants that help wind technicians troubleshoot from technical manuals. Ana: architectural designer for homes; leads the dashboard's design and usability. Goal: AI answers on spacecraft fire safety that designers can trust, with every claim citing its source and page, and facts kept separate from inference. Skills: AI workflow design, technical document curation, user-centred design.
summary:
Spacecraft cabin materials are rated with a flame test on Earth. But NASA's own tests show that in low gravity some materials keep burning with less oxygen. One example: Ultem 1000, a plastic film, passes the Earth test up to 24% oxygen. In Moon-gravity tests at the same pressure, it passes only up to 19.9%. And NASA's plans for Moon habitats call for 34% oxygen.

Flame Atlas lets a spacecraft designer or safety engineer check that gap for their own cabin. Set your oxygen, pressure and airflow, or tap ISS, Airlock, Moon lander or Moon base. The dashboard ranks NASA's combustion experiments by how close their tests are to your cabin, summarizes each one, charts what burned and what went out, and compares a material's Earth limit with its results in orbit and in reduced gravity. It holds 887 test results on 42 materials from NASA's PSI database, NASA reports and published papers, each with its source and page.

An SI assistant interprets our curated documents. Its answers cite source pages and keep data apart from inference. In a blind evaluation of 26 questions it scored 19 correct, 7 partial, 0 wrong.

It shows evidence and margins. The verdict stays with the engineer.
details:
Who it is for

A spacecraft designer or safety engineer choosing materials, cabin air or ventilation. Their question: is my material's Earth fire rating (NASA-STD-6001 Test 1) enough for this cabin, or is there evidence against it from tests in orbit or in reduced gravity?

Try it in one minute

  1. The page opens ranked for the Moon base cabin. Tap Airlock: the experiments re-rank.
  2. Switch to Material and pick Ultem 1000 (PEI). The card and the charts put its Earth rating next to its reduced-gravity results.
  3. Tap "What do the papers add?" on the card (answers at once), or a "Try" question in the chat (about 25 seconds).

What it does

  • Ranks NASA's combustion experiments by how close their tests are to your cabin's oxygen, pressure and airflow.
  • Summarizes each experiment on a card and lists the tests behind every number, each with its source and page. The selection downloads as CSV, for use in modelling.
  • Charts the results by oxygen, airflow and pressure. A dot is one test; a diamond is a burn limit reported by a paper. Larger marks match your conditions.
  • Compares a material's Earth limit with its results in orbit and in reduced gravity, and shows where your cabin sits between them.
  • Interprets: an SI assistant is instructed to answer only from our curated documents, to cite source and page for each point, to keep "from the data" and "inferred" in separate lists, and to say what the documents do not cover. You can attach a material datasheet. The chat also covers NASA's smoke-detection and fire-suppression experiments.

What NASA's data gave us

  • PSI, the 24 Combustion Science records: objective, platform, dates and DOI. They became the ranked Experiment list.
  • PSI-26 BASS and PSI-25 BASS-II (PSI test matrices and published reports): 266 test results, each with the conditions its log gives. They became marks on the charts.
  • PSI-20 ACME BRE and PSI-98, 99, 100 Saffire I–III, with their published results: 185 more tests, including the ones closest to the Moon base cabin.
  • 27 documents from the NASA Technical Reports Server: Earth limits, the lunar and Martian gravity tests (PSI has none yet), Saffire IV–VI, SoFIE, and the atmospheres behind the four cabin buttons.
  • The Researcher's Guide to ISS Combustion Science: background for the experiments that have no test results on the charts.

How we checked it

A blind evaluation of the assistant: 26 questions with answer keys tied to source pages, some about things the documents do not hold. SI drafted the questions and keys from the sources; two independent SI graders marked every answer and checked the cited pages against the PDFs. Result: 19 correct, 7 partial, 0 wrong. Details are in the repository README.

Benefits and intended impact

One of NASA's planning atmospheres for exploration habitats is 34% oxygen at 56.5 kPa: more oxygen and less pressure than on the ISS. The tool shows a designer what was tested near that cabin and what was not: 38 of the 887 results are near it, 31 of them from one gas-burner experiment, and only 19 of the 42 materials have any test in reduced gravity.

How it is creative

  • The ranking starts from your cabin. Change the cabin and the same experiments re-rank.
  • A material's Earth rating and its reduced-gravity results sit side by side on one card, with the tests behind each.
  • We graded the assistant's answers before trusting them, and we publish the result with its weak points.

What we considered

  • Designers need evidence and margins. The card holds only computed facts, with no SI.
  • A test that does not report one of your conditions is shown as a possible match, not as a match.
  • We do not rank materials: the data is too thin for that.

What works today, and what is next

Today, test results come from six PSI investigations and 13 other test campaigns in NASA reports and journal papers, JAXA's FLARE among them. The other 18 PSI investigations (mostly droplets, gas flames and smoke) are listed with their record, and the chat can describe them. Next: add the test results of those 18 investigations to the charts, and add Moon- and Mars-gravity data once NASA publishes it in PSI.

How it works, tools and languages

A static page (HTML, CSS, JavaScript, no framework, on GitHub Pages) draws everything except the chat in the browser, from one data file. The chat is an n8n Cloud workflow that reads the same tests table, with Google Gemini 3.8 Flash and context caching. The data files are built with Python.

Use of SI

The idea, the question and the design are the team's own. We chose the sources, made the design decisions, ruled on every open point in the data and set up the evaluation. SI was a tool we directed:

  • In the app: Google Gemini 3.8 Flash answers typed questions from our curated documents. The page marks answers as AI-generated.
  • Building it: Claude (Anthropic) extracted facts and test rows from the sources with page numbers, and wrote the answers behind the buttons; a second SI pass checked the cited lines against their source pages before we signed off. Code and data files were written with Claude Code under our direction and review; the code files, the tests file and the prepared-answer files say so in their headers.
  • Checking it: SI drafted the evaluation questions and answer keys; the two graders were SI agents working blind and independently.
  • Text and video: SI helped draft and edit this text and assemble the video.
